okay, we have a new project in:
{ROOT}

we have the github repo in:
{ROOT}\2_Github repos

this is where we locally work.

the following folders are read only:
{ROOT}\2_Github repos\0_OLD
=old versions of the repo, for history


"{ROOT}\2_Github repos\1_day one, untouched version made by devs"
untouched version made by devs
=the untouched version of the repo from day one. we may never change anything here. this works as a baseline so that we know what the devs created before we came along as a tester,

"{ROOT}\2_Github repos\2_current version, read only"
=this is a read only version of the current version of the repo, as it would look on github.
Drift is possible when I have been lazy, but I will try to update them as often as possible

"{ROOT}\2_Github repos\3_WITH my tests"
=this is a version of the repo where we will create my test folders and my TEST-ci.yml file.
Here we may make changes, but only to things that belong to testing and our own TEST-ci.yml file, never any workflows made by the devs, and never any changes to the things the devs have made.
ONLY to things related to our tests in tests/ and TEST-ci.yml.

The tests MUST follow QA and TEST automation best practices.
They must also follow AAA pattern.
They must also be commented in clear, junior friendly non technical comments written in simple plain english that a Junior can understand.
The Tests/ folder MUST mirror the repo and be clear about what type of tests belong where, so there should be subfolders named after the different levels of the test pyramid, such as E2E/, UNIT/, API/.
The UNIT/ test folder must mirror the structure of the repo, same with API/ test folder.
The E2E/ test folder should contain subfolders be named after the test.

then finally we have:
"{ROOT}\2_Github repos\4_upload to github"
in this folder, you will create copies of the files that have been changed, in a folder that is named efter the days date and hour.
Thus as time goes along we will have many folders there, all named after the day and hour they where made.
The folders here must be easy to drag and drop into github without any second though, so they must maintain the correct structure and subfolder structure.
Only changed files shall be included in these subfolders named after the day and the hour - so everything that is unchanged is NOT copied over.
In addition, create a .md file with a clear commit title and message, written in plain simple english.
Example:
Title: Fix(SET-xxx): created 3 new tests
Message:
-fix: created the following the 3 tests:
test a: does a by doing xyz
test b: does b by doing the following:...
test c: this is a test for doing [insert what it does]



How the test cases must be named:
if they are unit tests: then name them after the file and function they're testing.
if they're API tests, name them after this convention: API-TEST-[name of the API being tested]-[unique numeric ID, starts at 000, goes to 001, 002 and so on].
This way we can track the API tests as they change over time.
Keep in mind that if we change a tests, that does not suddenly give it a new numeric ID, since it is still the same test, just changed.
if they're E2E Tests, name them like this E2E-[what flow they're testing]-[unique numeric ID, starts at 000, goes to 001, 002 and so on].

This way we can track the E2E tests as they change over time.

Keep in mind that if we change a tests, that does not suddenly give it a new numeric ID, since it is still the same test, just changed.


then after each session, create a HTML workbook where we can keep track of the tests.
we should be able to see which test case is related to which plan (.md file), if it is implemented, not implemented, partially implemented, superseeded by another test (in that case which), what the test does (in simple english that the juniors can understand), how it does it step by step (in simple english that the juniors can understand), why this test is needed (in simple english that the juniors can understand), which test file is related to this test, what level of test this is (UNIT, API, E2E).
You can create the tracibility HTML workbook in a new subfolder (named after the day and the hour) in:
"{ROOT}\3_test traceability"
as time goes on, we will have many folder named after the day and the hour they where made, thus we can track the tests over long periods of time.
Use the workbook in this folder (for ANOTHER SEPARATE PROJECT) as inspiration, so you have a baseline to reference:
C:\ExternalReferences\test-traceability\20260811

and for the HTML dashboard, use this OTHER project as reference for how it should look:
C:\ExternalReferences\html-dashboard\20260814-01


This MUST be done after each new change,
This MUST be enforced with LangGraph
(the langGraph files must all live in: {ROOT}\4_LangGraph for this project)


we also have an obsidian vault in:
{ROOT}\0_Obsidian vault
this works as the projects lasting memory, a 2nd brain of sorts.
You must document every session and conclusion in a smart manner here so that we can search through our old sessions, and so that the AI agent can keep track of everything we've done over long time horizons as this project stretches on day after day, year after year.
Maybe KV cache it if it makes search easier for you.
This updating of the vault is also a must, you may never forget this.

enforce these rules with langGraph to make sure they are 100% followed.
